data: First successful Mars lander; biology experiments
Skeleton entry for /fleet (PRD-012 v0.2 / Phase A scaffold). Builder + agency + first-flight per public sources. Specs and gallery TBD in later phases.
On Mars: Exploration of the Red Planet 1958-1978 (NASA SP-4212)

Viking 1 solved the problem nothing had solved: how to land on Mars and live. The Soviet landers before it had died within about twenty seconds of touchdown, returning only a featureless grey frame; Viking had to descend through an atmosphere too thin to rely on and too thick to ignore, and it did it with a first-of-its-kind sequence — an aeroshell to survive entry, a parachute for the middle of the fall, and throttled rocket engines to set its three legs down softly at the end. It was two machines in one, an orbiter to survey and relay and a lander to work the ground, and it carried the first laboratory ever sent to test another planet’s soil for life. Every Mars landing since has flown some version of the descent Viking proved.

The first successful Mars lander mission, on the surface from July 1976 through November 1982. Carried four biology experiments and returned high-resolution images of the Chryse Planitia plains. The Viking 1 / Viking 2 pair set the template for every Mars lander that followed.
First fully successful Mars landing; first long-duration surface science
Second US Mars surface lander (Utopia Planitia 1976-09-03). Twin of Viking 1 lander; ran biology, soil chemistry + meteorology until 1980
Lost during landing in 1999; the failure led NASA to review its “faster, better, cheaper” approach
Confirmed water ice in Martian soil
Last successful Soviet Moon mission — returned 170 g of Mare Crisium regolith 1976-08-22; last lunar sample return until Chang'e 5

First fully successful Mars surface mission. Viking 1 operated for over six years on the surface — the longest-duration surface mission until Opportunity (a rover) broke the record in 2010. It returned the first colour images from the Martian surface, conducted the first life-detection experiments (results famously inconclusive), and characterised the regolith and weather.

Operated 1,281 days at 48°N — the highest-latitude Mars surface mission until Phoenix. Detected the first frost on Mars in September 1977 — water ice confirmed — with an iconic high-resolution image captured in May 1979. The lander's biological experiments returned the same ambiguous results as Viking 1's: chemistry that mimicked metabolism, but without unambiguous biology.
